teaching.task: # Year 11 Chemistry M1 V27: Solubility. How can attractions explain whether a substance dissolves? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: Dissolving is a trade of attractions. The solute is the substance that dissolves, and the solvent is the liquid it dissolves in. First, solute particles are pulled away from each other. Second, solvent particles move apart to make room. Both steps take energy. Third, new attractions form between solute and solvent particles, and that releases energy. As a first prediction, a substance dissolves well when the new attractions are about as strong as the ones it gives up. If they're much weaker, it barely dissolves. Take salt in water. In the crystal, sodium ions and chloride ions attract each other strongly. But water is polar, with a slightly negative oxygen end, and slightly positive hydrogen ends. Water molecules turn their oxygen ends toward the sodium ions, and their hydrogen ends toward the chloride ions. These ion dipole attractions are strong enough to pull ions off the crystal, one by one. Each ion ends up wrapped in water molecules, called a hydration shell. Now try hexane. Hexane molecules are non-polar, so they have no charged ends to offer. An ion can distort the electron cloud of a nearby hexane molecule, but those attractions are far too weak to pull the ions apart. So salt doesn't dissolve in hexane.

(a) Energy and entropy: dissolving is favourable when the Gibbs energy change is negative; the enthalpy of solution can be slightly positive (NaCl about +3.9 kJ/mol; NH₄NO₃ about +25.7 kJ/mol) and dissolving still occurs because mixing increases entropy (OpenStax Chemistry 2e, section 11.1). Hence "about as strong", and the one grey tag. Non-polar solutes in water: the hydrophobic effect is largely entropic (water ordering); the "bad trade of hydrogen bonds for weak dispersion" is the site's and the syllabus-level explanation.
(b) NaCl: 36.0 g per 100 g water at 25 °C (PubChem, CRC), so about 360 g per kilogram (about a litre) of water.
(c) Iodine: 1.73 g per 100 g n-heptane at 25 °C (PubChem, HSDB); in water about 0.03 g per 100 g at 25 °C (CRC; PubChem's NIOSH entry gives 0.01%). scenes.teachingReason: Dissolving is a trade of attractions. The solute is the substance that dissolves, and the solvent is the liquid it dissolves in. scenes.teachingReason: Take salt in water. In the crystal, sodium ions and chloride ions attract each other strongly. But water is polar, with a slightly negative oxygen end, and slightly positive hydrogen ends. Water molecules turn their oxygen ends toward the sodium ions, and their hydrogen ends toward the chloride ions. scenes.teachingReason: Oil is made of large, mostly non-polar molecules. Here's the surprise. Oil and water molecules do attract each other, through dispersion forces. They don't repel.
